bullets: Forward guidance alone is just words without a credible balance-sheet signal — a revised view replacing an earlier belief that forward guidance was sufficient on its own.
Forward guidance only works if the market believes the central bank will follow through; credibility rather than the announcement itself determines whether guidance moves expectations.
Reliability of policy signal matters more than the policy itself — framed as the most underrated and contrarian piece of monetary policy, and the lens that cross-cuts every other trade-off.
Policy decisions look obvious in hindsight and impossible in real time; internalizing that asymmetry makes subsequent decisions easier rather than harder.

Risk management at the Fed is mostly about not breaking the institution — protecting institutional integrity rather than optimizing any single policy outcome, with second-order effects being the part most people miss.
Framing matters because it reveals which trade-offs are being made, turning implicit policy choices into explicit ones.
Iteration beats ambition as a starting point — pick one idea, run it for two weeks, and refine from there.
